transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (VelocIT CTO), Liam O'Connor (Eng Manager), Priya Singh (SRE), Noah Kim (Dev)
Recording ID: ff-2026-10-14-velocit-edgecases-001

Auto-generated summary (auto): demo of Redwood handling long context windows, high TPS streaming workloads, discussion of streaming backpressure and timeout strategies. Next steps captured.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. hey Maya, Liam, Priya, thanks for making time. we're gonna run through the edge-cases demo — long context, high TPS, streaming with backpressure, and how timeouts look. Samir and Jordan will lead the deep parts.
[00:12] Maya: thanks, Avery. curious about the hosting options — we have a mix of hosted and on-prem infra. latency is a big deal for convo flows. also security, obv.
[00:20] Avery: totally, we'll cover hosted vs dedicated vs private. quick ask: Priya, are you the SRE owner?
[00:25] Priya: yep, that's me. main concerns: sustained 2k TPS at peak for embeddings and 800 TPS for chat, plus 100k token contexts for some analytics pipelines — oh and streaming stability for partial responses.
[00:36] Samir: ok that's a great baseline. quick clarification, when you say 100k tokens are these single-message contexts or aggregated history?
[00:42] Priya: aggregated history, sometimes we stitch customer transcripts over time.
[00:46] Jordan: got it. quick note — in the demo we'll show the API and console where you can pin model versions, set batching and cache policies, and run our Optimize recommendations. we built some synthetic loads to show long-context behavior and streaming backpressure.
[01:00] Liam: can you show how backpressure is surfaced in streaming API? we hit odd timeouts previously with another vendor.
[01:06] Samir: sure, we'll walk it. also, want to flag that some transcriptions may say "KV cash" rather than KV cache, or Kube-ness instead of Kubernetes, so ignore small typos in the transcript.
[01:14] Maya: ha, noted.

[01:20] --- Demo start: API walkthrough (long context) ---
[01:20] Samir: opening the api demo. here's a multi-turn chat request using the /v1/chat/stream endpoint, we stream token deltas using chunked transfer. payload includes a pinned model (rwd-large-quant), context pointers, and a reference to our KV cache.
[01:35] Samir: sending a request that attaches a 75k token context. watch the console — you'll see the planner decide to use sparse context windowing and our prefix prefetch.
[01:48] (console screen share noise)
[01:50] Jordan: console shows the request routed to our dedicated pool in eu-west-1 because of the routing policy. you can see per-token latency and the KV cache hit ratio.
[02:02] Priya: hmm the KV cache hit is low, what's the reason?
[02:05] Jordan: in this sim we disabled aggressive caching to demonstrate cold-start behavior. Optimize would recommend prefix caching for your workload.
[02:12] Samir: note — for very long contexts we shard the sequence into segments and use a streaming recompute approach to reduce memory. that's why the API returns partial tokens while recompute continues.
[02:24] Maya: does that increase end-to-end latency for final token?
[02:27] Samir: there is slight increase for the final tokens but average latency stays lower under sustained load. we also have an optional async completion call if you want final aggregate only.

[02:40] --- High TPS load test ---
[02:40] Samir: switching to the TPS stress test. we ramp to 2k concurrent embedding requests and 800 chat TPS. watch the metrics: throughput, p50/p95/p99, and dropped connections.
[02:55] (synthetic load generator chatter)
[03:00] Jordan: we surfaced a small spike in p99 at 750ms when we hit a particular kernel path. our optimizer flagged a different kernel recommendation for longer sequences which dropped the p99 to ~420ms.
[03:12] Liam: how do you push that optimization to our dedicated pool?
[03:15] Samir: we can push a kernel profile via the model build config and rollout via the console — can be canary-tested at 10% then rolled to 100%.

[03:28] --- Streaming backpressure scenario ---
[03:30] Samir: now we'll simulate network congestion between client and the streaming endpoint to trigger backpressure. the client will read slowly causing TCP send buffers to fill. you'll see the server detect backpressure and apply adaptive batching and a queued response strategy.
[03:48] (timeout beeps in background)
[03:50] Priya: what does adaptive batching mean for ordering? we need strict order for our transcripts.
[03:55] Jordan: ordering stays deterministic per-request; backpressure may delay emission of partial tokens but we never reorder tokens within a stream. we also support checkpointed resume tokens if a connection drops.
[04:08] Maya: checkpoint resume sounds useful — what's the resume window?
[04:12] Samir: default is 60s for streaming resume tokens, configurable up to 5 minutes on dedicated. longer windows cost memory/kv-state.
[04:20] Priya: any guarantees for exactly-once delivery?
[04:23] Samir: streaming emits idempotent chunk IDs, clients can dedupe; exact once is hard over intermittent networks, but we provide strong-at-least-once with dedupe tokens.

[04:35] --- Timeout behavior and retries ---
[04:36] Jordan: next we show timeout policies. Redwood supports three layers: client-side timeout, gateway timeout, and model compute timeout. you can configure fallback policies — e.g., if compute times out at 15s, fall back to a smaller model or precomputed response.
[04:52] Liam: in the past another vendor just dropped the connection. will Redwood auto-fallback to cached answers?
[04:57] Samir: yes if you enable fallback policies in the route. Optimize will suggest when a fallback makes sense based on cost/quality tradeoffs.
[05:05] Maya: how do we evaluate quality regressions from fallbacks? we want alerts if fallback reduces answer quality below a threshold.
[05:11] Jordan: our Console ties into evals — you can set prompt-based tests and register quality baselines; when a fallback runs, it logs the event and runs the quick eval to compare. alerts can be emailed or routed to Slack.

[05:22] --- Security & deployments discussion ---
[05:23] Maya: security: SOC2, SAML SSO, KMS integration, and audit logs. we may need on-prem for regulated customers.
[05:30] Avery: we support SOC2, SAML, RBAC, KMS/HSM integrations, and an on-prem Private deployment. audit logs are available in Console with retention options. we'll attach the security pack after this call.
[05:40] Priya: for Private, what's the control plane model?
[05:43] Jordan: Private gives you a customer-managed control plane that talk to Redwood's operator — we can also do fully air-gapped installs. note that some managed features like Optimize recommendations require opt-in telemetry.
[05:55] Priya: can recommendations run locally? we try to avoid external telemetry.
[05:58] Samir: you can run Optimize locally in Private with a shipped binary; the hosted recommendations are extra if you want Redwood-managed signals.

[06:08] --- Customer Q&A and objection handling ---
[06:09] Liam: cost — how do we compare hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved capacity for our profile? we have spiky loads and long contexts so caching helps but memory costs rise.
[06:20] Avery: typical guidance: hosted is fastest to go live and simpler; dedicated gives unit cost predictability and better tail latency control. for spiky loads we recommend a hybrid routing policy: primary dedicated pool + hosted overflow.
[06:33] Maya: overflow to hosted raises data residency concerns though.
[06:36] Avery: yes, can do regional routing and VPC peering to keep data in-region, or keep overflow off for regulated workloads.
[06:42] Priya: curious about quantization artifacts on long context. do you lose generation fidelity?
[06:47] Samir: quantization affects local numeric precision but our kernel selection and attention approximations preserve most quality for long-context tasks; we recommend per-prompt evals which Optimize can generate.

[06:58] --- Live troubleshooting (brief) ---
[06:58] (Noah types in chat)
[07:00] Noah: we saw a 504 from your demo a second ago, any idea?
[07:02] Jordan: that was intentional in sim to show gateway timeout. the flow triggered fallback and then resumed with a smaller model. you should see a log entry in the Console with the fallback event id.
[07:12] Maya: can you show the log?
[07:14] Jordan: sure, pulling console logs — here's the event: fallback_id=fb-3372, route=eu-west-1/dedicated-pool, reason=compute_timeout_15000ms, fallback_model=rwd-small-quant.
[07:28] Priya: ok good to see full event payload. is that exportable to Splunk/Datadog?
[07:32] Samir: yes, we support log export via S3, direct Datadog/Datastore sinks, and webhooks.

[07:40] --- Wrap up / recap ---
[07:41] Avery: quick recap: we showed long-context handling (sharding + streaming recompute), high TPS behavior and kernel optimization, streaming backpressure (adaptive batching + resume tokens), and timeout/fallback policies tied into Console evals/alerts.
[07:56] Maya: this was helpful. next for us is to run a POC for the dedicated pool and validate resume tokens and fallback quality.
[08:03] Liam: please include the benchmark spreadsheet and a sample POC runbook.
[08:06] Avery: will do. Samir, anything else?
[08:09] Samir: I'll run the backpressure sim with your exact prompt set once you share it and we'll baseline p50/p95/p99 and token-cost.
[08:15] Maya: timeline — we want a pilot in the week of 2026-10-25 if possible.
[08:19] Avery: noted. we'll follow up with dates.
[08:22] Jordan: attaching links in the follow-up: 1) PPT: redwood-edgecases-demo.pdf, 2) bench spreadsheet: redwood-tps-bench-velocit.xlsx, 3) security pack link: /docs/security/redwood-security-pack-v3.pdf.
[08:33] Priya: will need the SAML flow diagram and KMS notes too.
[08:36] Avery: yep included.

[08:40] (end recording)
